<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="">
<p>I've been thinking about the virtues and vices of posting art online, so I decided to write about my relationship to art and the internet, and how it has evolved over time. I think the following is a good document of how I <em>feel</em> about the subject. I suspect some of my logic is fuzzy or faulty, though I&#39;m not quite sure where. If you can identify where I&#39;m thinking incorrectly, please let me know.  </p>
<p>As a teenager and young adult, I was indoctrinated into a couple baseline assumptions about making art in the digital age:</p>
<ul>
<li>When you make art, you should post it to the internet</li>
<li>The amount of engagement (likes on Instagram, notes on Tumblr) that a piece of art gets indicates how popular/good that piece is</li>
<li>Followers = credibility</li>
<li>Getting lots of followers will get you jobs in the animation and/or comics industries</li>
</ul>

<p>It&#39;s not that I thought other success conditions for art didn&#39;t exist, but I thought, on some level, getting into a gallery or a flesh and blood friend liking my comic felt like like consolation prizes. The internet was what mattered.  </p>

<p>As a teen on tumblr.com, none of my art was successful. I tried to make fan art, because that&#39;s what my friends who were popular online did, and it never worked out well for me. Bombing online like that in my teen years was terrible for my mental health, and bred a lot of insecurity. Later, in college, I started making autobiographical comics on a regular basis and posting them on Instagram. Because I thought that the algorithm rewarded frequent posting (and because I knew I had a follow-through problem I needed to work on), I developed a series of constraints for my work:  </p>

<ul>
<li>4-10 panels max</li>
<li>The panels had to be the size of post-it notes. That size mean that I can&#39;t get too fixated on details. The shape meant it fit perfectly onto an Instagram slideshow.</li>
<li>Each comic/post should be understandable as stand-alone story/object. Most people who find your work through the algorithm will not see your other work.</li>
</ul>

<p>A few of the initial comics got several thousand likes, which was the most attention I&#39;d ever received online. After that initial burst, my comics averaged out at around 120 likes. So I set my emotional expectations accordingly. If a comic got less than 100 likes, it probably wasn&#39;t very good. If it cleared 300, it did well. I spent an embarrassing amount of time looking at blog posts from marketing agencies about gaming the algorithm. In retrospect, I&#39;m pretty sure most of those blog posts were guesses and glorified kremlinology that existed mostly to sate a need for certainty. I wanted to know the rules of the game I was playing. Of course, the mistake was playing the game in the first place.  </p>

<p>Ultimately my posts got me nothing. I didn&#39;t get any internships, and I never received any monetary reward for my work. I think my comics were good for what they were, and some people got real value out of them. But the comics were too sloppy to be used as portfolio pieces or published in a comics collection. At the end of the day, I had made a bunch of comics that really only made sense as posts.  </p>

<p>After I graduated college, I set aside six months (which became two years) to be a &quot;regular person&quot;. I felt like my life had been warped by my focus on what I thought was the path to success in professional art, and I needed some time away from that to re-orient myself. I worked in food service, and as a street canvasser. I kept drawing in my sketchbook, but never posted my drawings. I stopped posting entirely. I experimented with journalism, but found that it was as risky of a career as art, and I didn&#39;t have the years of training and experience that I had with comics or animation.  </p>

<p>Last fall, I got a job teaching at LACMA, and started making comics again. Because I didn&#39;t want my autobio work to be my body of work anymore, I decided I was done with Instagram. I wanted to make comics that were comics first, and posts second. I made a Bluesky under a new username. I was going to start fresh.  </p>

<p>Six months later, I finished a 25-pager that is, without a doubt, the best comic I&#39;ve ever made. When I published it on itch.io, I announced the comic on my Bluesky account. That post has received one like, from my girlfriend. One person, a friend from college who found out about the comic via my announcement on my private Instagram, bought the comic on itch. About 10 other friends have bought copies from me in person.  </p>

<p>When I played the game, I didn&#39;t get the prize, and the game felt evil, so I stopped playing. Turns out, if you don&#39;t play the game, you also don&#39;t get a prize. I thought about applying to Short Run Seattle and CALA this year, but both of the application forms ask for social media and a portfolio site. I don&#39;t have either of those the way I used to. So I guess I need to play the game.  </p>

<p>Posting is gambling. An art career is also gambling. It&#39;s like in order to successfully make things and then show them to people, I need to buy a lotto ticket where the prize is a ticket to a larger lottery. The AI of it all only makes matters worse. Some of the smartest people in the world are working very hard right now to figure out how to get all the revenue from the gambling without ever having to give out any prizes. But they&#39;ve also curated a system where gambling is the only <label for="sn-option" class="margin-toggle">option.</label> </p>
  <input type="checkbox" id="sn-option" class="margin-toggle sidenote-number"/>
  <span class="sidenote">
    I know there's the indieweb, and blogging, and an entire non-centralized internet to be reckoned with. But ultimately I think the people, and the power, is still on social networks. I want that internet to exist (why do you think this website exists) but if I am earnestly trying to be successful, I think I have to incorporate social media.  
  </span>. 

<p>I want to make comics. I want to help other people make comics. I want to evangelize for the art form, and I want to be successful in the industry that surrounds the art form. But building a career as an writer/artist right now feels like walking into a volcano. In order to post again, and to post frequently, and to make good work, I will have to be giving up so much of my time, and therefore my life. Just to buy a lotto ticket that gets me another lotto ticket that gets me a lower-middle-class life.  </p>

<p>That said, if I fully focus on becoming a career educator, I think I&#39;ll have a chip on my shoulder for the rest of my life because I never really gave an art career a shot.  </p>

<p>I don&#39;t know what I&#39;ll actually do. Maybe I&#39;ll throw myself back into it. Maybe I&#39;ll just do what I can with the time I have. Like a poor man that buys a lotto ticket every week and prays for the day his number comes in. Even when he logically knows that there&#39;s better places to put his money, his time, and his hope.  </p>
